_source: Recovered from G-Wolves_Software_V1.0.20.07's shipped .NET binary; every byte below is observed, not guessed. Full provenance, the repaired-DPI story and what `_needsVerification` here means: docs/profiles/gwolves-hsk-pro-4k.md

match._note: The config endpoint is identified by a vendor usage page (0xffff observed) plus a feature report -- not by interface number, which was 7 on the dongle. VID/PIDs are hts_init's own constants.

transport._note: hts_send_cmd: feature report 65 bytes, report id 0, no checksum; accept iff reply byte 1 == 0xA1. Byte 2 payload length, byte 3 opcode (read = write + 0x80), byte 4 link flag, payload from byte 5.

linkProbe._note: Link flag is a property of the endpoint, not of where the mouse is: an ACK on the wrong flag still returns an all-zero payload. Probing both and keeping the one that answers with data is the only honest detection.

commands._note: Read opcode = write opcode + 0x80. `linkFlag: false` marks commands whose byte 4 is part of the sub-command, not a link flag. The reply echoes the request: length, opcode, flag, payload from byte 5.

dpi._note: 51 payload bytes need a longer settle than the scalar commands, or the reply sometimes arrives all-zero and an ignored write is indistinguishable from success. readModifyWrite so changing one stage never zeroes the others.

repairOnWrite.why: stage count of 0 makes the firmware write no stages at all; confirmed on hardware 2026-08-18

sleep._note: Sleep is a sub-command of opcode 0x02: byte 6 selects get (0x87) or set (0x07), value is u16be at bytes 7-8.

batteryPercent._note: A percentage for this model specifically: get_Battery_empty branches on product id, and the curve the vendor app applies differs per family. hskctl reports the byte unrounded.
batteryPercent._verified: Discharge confirmed on hardware 2026-08-19: 100 -> 81 overnight, ~2.4 points/hour

charging._note: rx[5] > 0. Flips within one sample of the cable going in / coming out, confirmed 2026-08-19.

connection._note: Observed 1 on the dongle; the cable reports 0.

ui.label: Polling rate
ui.description: How often the mouse reports its position

pollingRate._note: Measured by timing the mouse's own reports, none inferred: the register is not a formula. Raw 1..6 divide a 1000 Hz base; 32 and 64 are the 2000/4000 Hz high-rate codes.
pollingRate._uiOptionsNote: uiOptions is what the panel renders; `values` is the full set `hskctl set pollingRate <n>` accepts (200/333/167 Hz are real, settable, just not vendor-selectable).

ui.label: Lift-off distance
ui.description: How far above the desk the sensor keeps tracking

liftOffDistance._note: Raw 0 is rejected by the firmware -- the earlier 0/1 map was wrong in both directions.

ui.label: Motion sync
ui.description: Align sensor reads to the polling clock

sleepSeconds._note: SECONDS, confirmed by timing the mouse. The 30s step is what Sleep_update_ui positions its slider for; a value under 30 presumably selects 'off'.

debounceMs._needsVerification: read returns byte 0 of a 4-byte tuple while the write takes a row index -- the two are not the same number, so writing stays disabled until the table is modelled

activeDpiStage._note: rx[5], the stage the dpi-level combo drives. Stage switching is verified against hardware by the panel's runtime probe, never by this flag.

dpiStageCount._note: rx[6] -- how many stages the firmware writes out of the packet. Reads 0 on this mouse, which the repairOnWrite fix above handles.
dpiStageCount._needsVerification: writing it is untested on hardware; read, change the count, and check the mouse cycles that many stages before trusting the write

ui.label: DPI
ui.description: Stage 1 sensitivity; writes the Y axis with it, like the vendor app

dpiStage1._note: X axis of stage 1. dpiStage1Y rides the same packet, so the axes track together unless set apart.

dpiStage1Y._note: Y axis of stage 1. Writing it alone leaves X; writing X re-links them.

_pollingNote: Resolved. The vendor slider emits 1<<position, so positions 0..6 give raw 1,2,4,8,16,32,64. Measured: 1=1000, 2=500, 4=250, 32=2000, 64=4000 Hz. 4K is reachable and needs no separate mode.
